utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Can you call the case, Madam.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-95-11-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. May I have the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. For the Prosecution Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff accompanied by Case Manager Lakshmie Walpita.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence, please. Didn't you get the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We have some problems. [Interpretation] Everything is fine. Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honour. I am Defence counsel for the accused Martic. I am Predrag Milovancevic from Belgrade. Together with me is attorney Vuk Sekulic, also from Belgrade, my assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the right channel. 4 would be all right? Okay. I hope 4 is the right one. I wasn't on the right one. Excuse me for that. Mr. Martic, please, can you hear me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, we are here now for the -- another occasion of the Status Conference. I had heard about how is the situation of the case. I'm glad that the disclosure is working, not without some problems but with a good pace. I am very glad of all that the Defence now can go through the materials that have been passed over by the Prosecution. It seems that you have some problems with indexes but I am confident and I believe that you will be on the way to make a resolution for this problem. Another aspect that has been very, let's say, rejoicing for me even is that on the agreement of the facts if I have well understood, I have seen that the Defence has made known to the Prosecution that there are quite a lot of agreement on some of the facts but very few exceptions. So I am very glad about that and I hope that that will be some aspect that could -- that remains more expeditious and a fair solution of the case. I have heard about some problems about the pre-trial brief of the Defence, especially on the aspects of the translation of these for the use of the accused. Above all, I have to remark just for the information of the counsels for the Defence that the translation of the -- in the pre-trial stage of the Prosecutor brief is not considered like a normal course of action. Let me remind you what has been said not so much time ago and is still valid nowadays in the case of Prosecutor versus Pasko Ljubicic. It has been said in the decision adopted on the 20th of November, 2002, that: "Pursuant to the Statute and the Rules, and based on the mainstream of the existing judicial practice as referred to above," and they had made a reference before, "the current general standard regarding translation of documents during the pre-trial stage of the proceedings requires that the following material be submitted to the Accused in a language he understands: "a copy of the indictment according to Article 21, paragraph 1 and paragraph 4(a) of the Statute and Rule 53 bis (B) in combination with Rule 47 (G) of the Rules; "a copy of the supporting material which accompanied the indictment against the Accused and all prior statements obtained by the Prosecutor from the Accused, irrespective of whether these items will be offered at trial, in accordance with Rule 66(A)i of the Rules." Thirdly, "statements of all witnesses (either in hard copy or in audio format) whom the Prosecutor intends to call to testify at trial along with all written statements taken in accordance with Rule 92 bis, and statements of additional Prosecution witnesses when a decision is made to call those witnesses --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down, Your Honour, when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I apologise. Excuse me. Should I repeat or -- no, it's okay. Fourthly, "discovery material which appeared in a language understood by the Accused at the time it came under the Prosecution's custody or control, pursuant to Rule 66(B) of the Rules." Fifthly, "exculpatory material disclosed by the Prosecutor according to Article 68 of the Rules; and..." Sixth and finally, "written decisions and orders tendered by the Tribunal." I have read that exactly as it was pronounced in this decision in the Ljubicic case because I want to emphasise and to make sure that you understand that the Prosecution brief is not included among the documents that has to be translated for the accused. If any problem could be determined by this, not habit or not custom or not translated in that, I would say that it would be clearly taken out of the picture because I know that not only is that given in English but also that Mr. Sekulic is absolutely proficient in the knowledge of English, so that he can conduct to the accused the content of the brief presented by the Prosecution. On the other side I have to remind you that this Chamber has allowed to the Defence extra time to give an answer to present its brief that was supposed to be handed in in September. And now has time extended until, I believe, the 1st of November. I would also insist on the case of this brief that it's not a document in which it has to be very much involved as a contributor the accused himself, because he's weighted more with legal problems that -- legal issues more than with the factual aspects of the case. So it's more for the counsel of the accused than for the accused himself to take care of the content of this brief. If you may allow me, I'm going to refer to Rule 65 ter F in which it is said what should be the content of this Defence brief. It would refer as is said first to, "in general terms, the nature of the accused's defence;" Secondly, "the matters with which the accused takes issue in the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief." That means that is also a legal aspect which is being made reference to here. And thirdly, "in the case of each such matter," and referring to the previous requirement, "the reason why the accused takes issues with it." So as you see, and of course you know, but I wanted to emphasis this aspect. It's more legal aspects that are involved in the production of this Defence brief than a reference to the facts that of course had been gathered before in the case and are going to be presented as a matter of proof during the hearing of the case. So as far as I know the matters in which I can, well, communicate with the parties so as to increase and to impose your communication so as to -- make quick events in dealing with the case. Now I have to refer especially to Mr. Martic. Please, Mr. Martic, would you tell me your situation, your medical and health situation is in good condition or do you have any trouble or any problem that you would like to inform me about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I naturally have some problems but not concerning my stay here. Everything is fine concerning my detention. However, I have problems with my defence and let me be clear about it. I am happy with my Defence counsel, but I'm not happy with the treatment because this looks like a discrimination. I don't know what other term I could use except for discrimination. Let me clarify this. The Prosecution alleges that I held the highest positions in the country, prime minister and so on, and when it comes to registry's position to my defence then they treat me as a reserve policeman. Even had I been a reserve policeman, the allegations in the indictment are much broader. I am a lawyer myself and I have to tell you that this boils down to discrimination. I'm denied all my human rights and all other rights. On the other hand, Your Honour, those who expelled my people from Croatia are still in highest public offices. Thousands of civilians were killed under the protection of the United Nations and no investigations have been launched until this day against those people. It seems as though no indictments will ever be raised against them. The chief Prosecutor meets with those people, sees them here as the most honourable guests, all the way up to ministers in the government, vice-presidents of the government, and so on. So those are the people who were involved in these crimes before the international protection forces came and afterwards. And how did they protect my people? We all know because my people were ethnically cleansed. In addition to that there are all these problems about my defence rights being denied to me. And when we take all of that into account, what is happening here and what is happening back there, then we can see very clearly that this is a case of pure discrimination. So this is what troubles me. Other than that, my health and detention conditions are satisfactory, as I've stated in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: You may sit down but I'm going to answer you in a different way. First, I'm going to answer you about your second problem you initiated. It's not for me to take a decision about what cases and what facts to be prosecuted. You may get in relation with the Prosecution office, and then perhaps take or accept what you have to say about these facts. You believe under the command of the United Nations -- believe have been committed as delinquency acts. That's one point. But, on the other, I am very surprised because if I had well understood you, you mean that all your human rights have been de-negated to you. That seems to me very peculiar and besides when you say you have been treated in a discriminatory way, I am wondering by whom. You say that you are not happy with your defence, does that mean that you are not -- I mean that that you are discriminated against by your own defence? I don't think so. No? Please speak up. It's -- my being here is exactly -- one of the reasons of my being here is to hear you about whatever complaints you may have and try to right up the situation. Your own defence against you, is discriminating you. I couldn't believe that in principle. But tell me if you have any special complaint. I see that you laugh and I see that Mr. Milovancevic also was laughing at that possibility, so it makes me believe that nothing of the kind exists. Tell me, please. Don't laugh and tell me -- it's a very serious issue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm laughing because this is the third time you've put the same question to me. You asked me whether I'm content and happy. I'm more than happy and content because these people are defending me properly. But I wanted to point out to you this disproportion between the Prosecution on the one hand who has piled up a lot of allegations in the indictment as to the positions I had. So that's one hand, and then on the other hand we have the registry who is denying me my full right to defend myself. They are not providing me everything I am entitled to. I want to put out a proper defence but I am unable to. And on the other hand you keep asking me whether I'm happy with how things are going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: What you say is a very tremendous way of informing me about the situation. First of all, the Prosecution is doing its work in a normal conduct; I mean in a normal way, if I way say so. So I don't understand why because you are accused by the Prosecution, you are mistreated or discriminated against; that's not the case. I could expect that in the way you are treated in the Detention Unit or by other persons in this Tribunal, you may complain. But exactly the fact that I am asking you and trying to know about what's the situation from you is clear proof that you are treated like everybody else. You haven't been postponed to have this Status Conference, to be heard whenever it has been necessary. So I don't understand exactly. If you can be more precise about what rights you have been attacked and has been damaged by whenever -- whoever has been the author of that, I may begin to think about that. So please tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me clarify once again. The rights that have been denied to me, the funds, the funds to finance the work. So far my Defence has worked pro bono. They have not been paid for months now. As for the Prosecution, now that you've raised that issue, let me say that I served as president of the republic that doesn't exist anymore. That was the greatest example of ethnic cleansing in the 20th century, what happened to my people there. And to this day, nobody has complained about that. Carla Del Ponte's delighted with the cooperation she has established with Stipan Mesic and others who were involved and who issued orders for crimes to be committed against civilians while the UN was there. And of course I'm not happy with that. Nobody else has raised the issue but me. Those people are gone. They were either killed or they immigrated to other continents. So how can I be happy. There have been no indictments concerning Miljevac Plateau, concerning Malenica [phoen], Operation Flesh, where hundreds and hundreds of civilians were killed mercilessly, and nobody seems to care. And the more dead Serbs, the better. That seems to be the position they've taken. So what does that amount to if not discrimination? And here I am standing trial here for command responsibility, but I'll let the Prosecution prove their charges. I will have to prove my innocence, but so far I have been denied the resources to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: I have let you speak but I have to oppose very much what you have said. I'm not going into a contradiction with you, but just realise that what you have said about being discriminated by the Prosecution has really nothing to do with the behaviour of the Prosecution. The Prosecution is treating you like everybody else that has been brought under the jurisdiction of this court. Your ideas or your beliefs about who has to be subjected to the jurisdiction of this Tribunal is something very, very different and very separated on whatever -- and I would say that I wouldn't tolerate that the Prosecution could be accused of discrimination because of this kind of view of the situation. You are not treated, as far as I know, unless you give me other special reason that you are treated in a different or worse way that other accused in -- under this Tribunal. So unless you offer to me some case of discrimination the views that you maintain about who has to be accused or not, they have nothing to do with the behaviour of the Prosecution to be considered as a form of discrimination. So, perhaps you have different views but I am to be neutral and I try to be neutral and I hope I'm going to be neutral so as not to upset some particular views which I understand that you may maintain in your situation but I -- cannot be accepted by the Tribunal. Well, unless the parties have another question to raise and perhaps Mr. Milovancevic intended to speak, I could finish the -- so you want to speak. Please tell me -- tell us, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Your Honour, yes. I would just like to clarify a certain point. The complaints made by Mr. Martic today, his objections, relate to a problem that is not directly concerned with the work of the Prosecution. And perhaps Mr. Martic drew a parallel there which seemed to him to be logical. What he referred to was the fact that the Defence at the last Status Conference and before you, too, raised a problem and that was the absence of funds, the absence of resources, which has led to a situation -- and I think that that's what Mr. Martic had in mind when he raised the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Milovancevic, before you go on on this subject, I have to tell you and to remind you that the position that may be taken by this Chamber and by myself on this matter is not at the time possible. You know that you have placed an appeal and the decision is now at the level of the Appeals Chamber who are going to give you the answer that you are looking for. Besides, I know that you have repeatedly complained about the lack of funds, but I have some date of my own and I had found that all in all and so far until perhaps March or until the last few weeks you have received $277.000 plus. To go with that I wondered if with this which is a tremendous amount of money you haven't been able to go too far away, but I think it's really very important amount of money. On the other aspect, you I think had said -- brought about in the previous 65 ter meeting you had had this morning the possibility of getting some people to help you. And I think that even the Prosecution has told you that perhaps you may engage somebody, a student, that would be capable enough to go through the huge amount of documents that you have to deal with now and perhaps that is a good suggestion. But I am sorry. I would have heard you if I could give you an explanation or a solution to your problem. Unfortunately it's not the case for me. You have to apply and you have already applied and you have to wait for the decision of the Appeals Chamber. Do you think there is something else I can help you, please tell me, but not about this. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The facts and figures as to the money spent has provided -- later on that has been provided by the registry and it is for two Defence teams dating from the time that Mr. Martic is in detention. The first Defence team -- as I say there are two Defence teams. We inherited the first Defence team and the first team spent most of the money so that we have had 50 per cent of the resources allotted to us. Now it is the secretariat which decides how the work of the Defence counsel will be paid and the level of the case. And depending on the complexity of the case, all the other matters are decided. So I don't think that the conduct on the part of the registry is correct and proper because it draws attention from the real problems. If I may be allowed to say one more thing, Your Honour, I am not dealing with my complaints but you were informed that we received a new deadline by the 1st of November and you have told us what it says in the rules. The Defence did not ask a deferral of the deadline because from May to September it didn't have enough time to work, to get through its work. Now the extended deadline by the Trial Chamber, given the explanation that the Prosecution brief is so long that the Defence will have to have to have enough time to study it, and the Defence is now faced with the question of resources. Because since March it has had no funds for work. So the situation is quite a drastic one in view of all these problems, but I won't dwell on that anymore. The report provided by the registry is -- could be said to be a proper one, if the -- but it is not in keeping with the rules. And we should look at how much each Defence team costs and then we can go into the figures. But this is for two and a half years, 30 months which means 30 months makes it $9000 a month for four Defence counsels, four attorneys working on a case of this caliber. Now, if we deal in arithmetic, and of course that is not the crucial point on which the Defence relies, the Defence is nonetheless in a very difficult position now, Your Honour, because we have to respond to the pre-trial brief in the best possible way, top quality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, excuse me again, I have to interrupt you. I am really sorry for you but I cannot give you any relief on this matter. I know you have been working only since December of 2002, which makes less than 2 years. And perhaps you received a limited amount of the money that was attributed for the case. But also remember that the registry gives you an extra money for the level of the case. On the other side I have to commend the way in which you are behaving with the case and you are working, and that is something to be recognised and I feel very happy about that. But I'm sorry I cannot give you a solution for the other problem. So please let's stop here about that. Even it doesn't mean that I don't appreciate the effort that you and your team are doing for the expeditiousness and the fairness of the case. Some other aspect?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm grateful to you for those words. The Defence merely wished to inform the Trial Chamber of the fact that we are in a situation in which we have been left without funds since March. And in June we had two highly productive meetings, one with Madam Prosecutor, that is to say Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, where we dealt with key questions so that the Defence is working in the best possible way, in the only way possible for it to organise itself to help the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution and first and foremost the accused, of course. But what is troubling the Defence at this point in time, Your Honour, is the fact that we now have a lot of talk about money of the Defence. It is money that the accused should have for the purposes of his Defence counsel. So once again, this is a drastic situation. We have not received funds for six months. We are going to inform the embassy of Yugoslav and the UN Secretary-General as well as the lawyers or the bar association of Europe and the government of the country whose citizen Mr. Martic is. Because it is a question of paramount importance, the kind which merits this move. It is of great interest to the accused and it involves the registry, of course, as well. It is a violation of the rights and so the Defence counsel cannot bypass the ethics of lawyers at the bar. So we do wish to write the best quality response to the pre-trial brief. But as I say, we have been left out resources to carry out investigations. It is a very lengthy pre-trial brief to which we have to respond, whereas our funds have been cut off. The Prosecution is continuing its work and in a case of this complexity, that is quite normal, the fact that they are continuing their work. We are not asking for a decision from you but we'd like you to understand the difficult we find ourselves in. We merely wish to inform you of them and there are matters that the Defence cannot consciously undertake and have it be at the detriment of the client whom we represent. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: I do understand what you have conveyed to me and I realise there are problems you have to go through, of course. But I commend you to take these views you have expressed so far to me to the Appeals Chamber so in a way to find a solution that would be in your interests. May I ask the Prosecution if they have any special matter that it wants to be raise here, now?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, as Mr. Harhoff obviously has informed you about what was said in the 65 ter Conference, I do not need to repeat anything. The only additional thing that I could say is in relation to the agreed facts. The Defence had actually today handed us their proposals. And as I looked through them we have actually already reached agreement on 29 important facts and three more are forthcoming. Actually we are only discussing at the moment one more fact. And otherwise we have actually found a very good agreement and I think in the very near future we will pass a joint motion to you with these agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much to the representative of the Prosecution because it's a great advancement for the position of the case that you announced to the Chamber. So I am very grateful and very glad that that has been achieved by both parties in the way of the solution for the case. Would you have any other suggestions to make now before we end this Status Conference? If it is not the case, I have to announce that a new Status Conference would be held in 120 days' time which makes us to think about January of the next year. I hope that in the meantime the Defence would be able to present the brief that it is required to present in due time, and that perhaps we'll be -- I mean the case in the pre-trial stage could be finished by January, but if not you know that in this moment we will meet again. So the meeting is adjourned. I thank you all for your presence and above all to the interpreters also as well. Thank you. ---Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at 4.26 p.m.
